draft.title: Crafting images
card: An image is language that helps a reader see, hear, touch, taste or smell something. It might be a simile, a metaphor or a plain detail.
one readers have met many times, such as "as busy as a bee". It is quickly passed over, so it adds little.
a specific, new picture, such as "the bus queue shuffled like a tired zip". It makes the reader stop and notice.
Writers often choose a central image and return to it. Each return adds meaning, so the image gathers weight as the piece goes on.
draft.remember: A fresh, specific image grabs a reader. A repeated one gathers meaning.

a.q: Which line contains the freshest, most specific image?
opts: The kitchen smelled of burnt toast and wet dog
The kitchen was as cold as ice
The kitchen was a hive of activity
The kitchen was very unpleasant
a.why: Burnt toast and wet dog are specific details that a reader can smell and picture. "As cold as ice" is the most tempting wrong answer, but it is a familiar phrase that readers pass over quickly.
a.clue: Which line gives details you could not guess in advance?

b.q: Priya begins her story with a cracked blue teacup, and brings it back when her grandmother is ill and again at the funeral. What is the effect of returning to the teacup?
opts: It gathers meaning and links to the story's feelings
It shows that Priya has run out of new ideas
It makes the plot move faster at each return
It shows that the teacup is a familiar image
b.why: Each return places the teacup in a new moment, so it comes to stand for the family's loss. Repetition does not make it a familiar image, because the teacup itself is specific. Freshness and repetition work together here.
b.clue: Think about what the teacup is near each time it appears.

a.best: The kitchen smelled of burnt toast and wet dog

b.best: It gathers meaning and links to the story's feelings

problems.detail: Too easy for Year 12 Advanced. Two distractors are obvious clichés and one ('very unpleasant') contains no image at all, so the answer can be picked without real judgement about freshness.
Fairly easy for Year 12. The distractors ('run out of new ideas', 'plot move faster') are implausible, so the question barely tests the idea of a recurring image gathering meaning.

proposal.title: Crafting images
card: An image is language that helps a reader see, hear, touch, taste or smell something. It might be a simile, a metaphor or a plain detail.
one readers have met many times, such as "as busy as a bee". It is passed over quickly. Adding words, as in "busy as the busiest bee", does not make it fresh.
a new, specific picture, such as "the bus queue shuffled like a tired zip". Exact details beat vague words: "burnt toast" does more than "a strange smell".
Writers often choose a central image and return to it. Each return adds meaning, so the image gathers weight. This is not a cliché, because the image is the writer's own.
proposal.remember: Make an image new and exact, then let it return and grow.

a.q: Which line contains the freshest, most specific image?
opts: Her voice was thin as the last scrape of jam in a jar
Her voice was as soft as the very softest of silk
Her voice had a strange, eerie and haunting sound
Her voice cut through the noisy room like a knife
a.why: The jam jar simile is new and exact: a reader can picture that thin, scraping sound. The silk line is tempting because it adds words, but it is still the familiar "soft as silk". The eerie line piles up vague adjectives without a picture, and the knife is a cliché.
a.clue: Strip away the extra words. Have you heard the comparison before?

b.q: Priya's story opens with a cracked blue teacup at her grandmother's table. It returns when her grandmother is ill and after the funeral. Why return to it?
opts: Each return adds meaning, so the cup comes to carry loss
It repeats one fixed meaning so readers do not forget it
Repeating it turns it into a cliché that readers skim
It mainly reminds readers what the teacup looks like
b.why: Each time the teacup appears in a new moment, it takes on more meaning, so by the end it holds the grandmother and the loss of her. The fixed meaning option is tempting, but a central image grows rather than staying the same. It is not a cliché either, because it is Priya's own image.
b.clue: Does the teacup mean the same thing at the funeral as at the start?

a.best: Her voice was thin as the last scrape of jam in a jar

b.best: Each return adds meaning, so the cup comes to carry loss
